text: Okay. Quick question.
Someone hands you forty dollars. What do you buy?
New shoes? A game? Dinner out?
Researchers asked ninety-eight working adults exactly that.
Only two percent said: I'd use it to buy back some time.
And that might be the best happiness deal most of us ignore.
Let's talk about buying time.
As the world got richer, people started feeling poor in something else. Time.
And that time stress is linked to less happiness, more anxiety, and trouble sleeping.
Researchers call it a time famine.
So they asked: can money buy some of that time back?
Your neighbor pays someone to clean. Lazy? The data says... happier.
Researchers surveyed over six thousand people in the US, Canada, Denmark and the Netherlands.
One question. In a typical month, do you pay someone to do the daily tasks you dislike?
The people who did were more satisfied with their lives.
And it wasn't a rich-people thing. The link didn't depend on income.
They even asked eight hundred eighteen millionaires. A big share spent nothing on it at all.
Now, when people felt short on time, their life satisfaction dropped.
For people who bought time, that drop was much smaller. Like a shield.
So... still think your neighbor's lazy?
But a survey can't prove cause. So they ran an experiment.
Sixty working adults in Vancouver. Two weekends in a row. Forty dollars each weekend.
One weekend, the rule was: buy a thing for yourself.
The other weekend: buy something that saves you time.
At five p.m., the phone rang. How are you feeling?
The time weekend won. A better mood, and less time stress.
And the mood boost ran through that drop in time stress.
So it works. But almost nobody thinks of it. Not even the experts.
Thirty current and future policymakers at Harvard were asked how to spend twenty-one dollars of aid for working women in Nairobi.
Only six percent thought of buying those women time. Offered three programs, twenty-six of the thirty picked cash.
One thousand and seventy working moms in Nairobi. Free laundry, or cash?
These moms already worked about forty hours a week for pay. And about forty more, unpaid, at home.
For three weeks, some got free cooking or laundry services. Some got the same value in cash. Some got nothing extra.
The researchers bet on time.
Then... everyone felt better. All three groups. About the same.
Free time didn't beat cash. And neither beat getting nothing extra.
So, free laundry, or cash? The honest answer: it didn't matter.
Now, honesty time.
A 2022 survey of over fifteen thousand Americans found the link again. Even for people living paycheck to paycheck.
But it was small. About half the size of the boost linked to giving to charity.
So buying time looks real. But it's a small nudge, not magic.
So here's what you can try this week.
One. Pick the chore you dislike most, and price out skipping it. Just once.
Two. Next time money lands in your lap, ask: could this buy me time?
Three. Count the minutes. If forty dollars buys back two hours, notice how that feels.
So. Forty dollars. New shoes... or your Saturday back?
Buy time, not things.
Subscribe, and go buy back one hour this week.
